text: Go outside your classroom. Stand still for two minutes.

The place may look very ordinary. But living things are all around you. Grass is growing through a crack in the path. A crow sits on the wall. Ants move in a line along the edge of a step. One tree has wide leaves. The tree next to it has thin ones.
Nobody planted most of these. Nobody arranged them. And no two of them are exactly the same.
This chapter is about that variety. How much of it is there? How do we make sense of it? And why are the living things in one place so different from the living things in another?
Observe the illustration. How many kinds of living things can you find? Which might you miss if you were walking quickly?
2.1 The Variety Around Us

Most of us walk past living things without really seeing them. We see a tree. But we do not see that its leaves are pointed, and the next tree's leaves are round. We hear birds. But we do not hear that three different birds are calling.
Looking carefully is a skill. Like any skill, it gets better with practice.
That is what the first activity is for.

The setup
**You will need:** a notebook, a pencil, a water bottle.
**What to do:**
1. With your teacher, spend one period in a park, a garden, a field or any open ground near your school.
2. Walk slowly. People who are in a hurry find very little.
3. Look, and also listen. Close your eyes for thirty seconds. How many different sounds can you count?
4. Do not pluck leaves or flowers. Do not disturb any animal. You may pick up leaves that have already fallen.
5. Copy the headings of Tables 2.1 and 2.2 into your notebook. Add a row for each plant or animal you observe.
**Safety:** Stay with your group. Do not touch any animal. Do not put your fingers into holes or under stones.

Write down what you really see, not what you think you should see. If you do not know the name of a plant, describe it instead. For example: "small plant, three leaves together, near the water tap". Was it harder to spot the plants or the animals? Why?
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.
A dash in a sample table means that the observation has not been recorded. It does not prove that the feature is absent. A plant without visible flowers today may flower in another season.
The drawings help you compare the plants. They are not drawn to a common scale; use your own observations to compare their actual heights.

Table 2.1: Plants you observed
Name / description | Stem | Leaves | Flowers | Anything else
Common grass | Soft and thin | One thin leaf at a time | — | Grows in a thick patch
Tulsi | Hard and thin | Leaves in pairs, facing each other | Small, pinkish purple | Smells strong when rubbed
Neem | Hard and thick | Many small leaves on one stalk |  |
Grass                         Tulsi                         Hibiscus
When your table has a few rows, read down the columns. Do not read across. The differences show up in the columns.

Some stems bend easily between two fingers. Some do not bend at all. Some leaves grow one at a time along the stem. Others grow in pairs, facing each other. Flowers are different in colour, in shape and in smell.
**What do you notice?** Were any two plants in your table the same in every column?
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.
A sound is useful evidence too. You may hear a bird hidden in a tree even when you cannot see its colour or shape.

Table 2.2: Animals you observed
Name / description | Where you saw it | Doing / eating | How it moved | Anything else
Crow | On a wall, then a tree | Pecking at something | Walks, then flies | Carried a twig away
Ant | Along the edge of a step | Carrying a crumb | Walks | Six legs; followed the ant in front
Animals are harder to record than plants. The reason is simple. They move, and many of them move away from you. So sitting still and watching finds more than walking about.

Now look down your table. Some animals live on the ground. Some live in trees. Some live in water, and some under stones. They eat very different things. They move in different ways — walking, flying, crawling, swimming, hopping.
The variety of living things found in one region is called its **biodiversity**.
Your school ground has its own biodiversity. So does a pond. So does a forest, a seashore, and even the soil in a flowerpot.
You looked for one period. Do you think you found most of the living things there? Or only a small part of them?
Living Things Need Each Other
The living things in a place are not just sharing space. They are joined to each other.

A tree gives shade. Small plants that cannot take strong sunlight grow in that shade. Birds build nests in its branches. They eat insects from its bark. A bird eats a fruit, flies away, and drops the seed far from the tree. The seed grows into a new tree there. Old leaves fall and rot into the soil. That soil feeds the next plant.
Now take one part away. The others feel it. If the insects go, the birds have less food. If the tree goes, the shade goes, the nests go, and the falling leaves go too.
One connection can lead to another. Fallen leaves provide food for small organisms in the soil. As those leaves break down, nutrients return to the soil and can be taken up by roots.
When you compare answers, draw arrows in your notebook between the living things you chose. Write a word beside each arrow, such as food or shelter, to explain the connection.

Choose any one living thing from Table 2.1 or Table 2.2. Write two things it needs from other living things. Write two things that other living things get from it. Compare your answers with a partner who chose something else. Could the living thing you chose stay alive on its own, in an empty place with nothing else living there?
2.2 Making Sense of the Variety
Your two tables now hold a long, untidy list. Nature really is like that. But it is hard to study anything from an untidy list.

Think of a shop that sells stationery. Suppose everything was thrown into one big heap. Finding one pen would take an hour. Shops do not do this. Pens are kept with pens. Notebooks are kept with notebooks. Geometry boxes are kept together.
Once things are in groups, two things become easy. You can find what you want. And you can see what the shop has.
Scientists do the same with living things. Putting things into groups by the features they share is called **grouping**.

The setup
**You will need:** old magazines or newspapers, scissors, glue, small cards.
**What to do:**
1. Cut out pictures of plants and animals. Paste one on each card. Try to make at least thirty cards in the class.
2. Work in groups of five or six. Put all your cards together.
3. Sort the pile into groups. You decide what the groups will be.
4. Write down, in one line, the rule you used.
5. Now mix all the cards again. Sort them a second time, using a completely different rule.
**Safety:** Use scissors carefully, with your teacher’s guidance.

Keep your sorting rule visible. If a card is difficult to place, explain what makes it difficult instead of hiding it in a convenient pile. An awkward example can show you how to make the rule clearer.
Compare both your sortings with another group's. Did any two groups in the class use the same rule?
There Is No One Correct Sorting
When the class compares answers, something surprising happens. Almost every group sorted the same cards differently. And none of them were wrong.
One group may have put plants on one side and animals on the other. Another may have used size. Another may have used where the living thing lives, or what it eats, or whether it has flowers.
Some ways of grouping

This is important to understand. It is easy to think that living things come with group names already fixed on them. They do not. We make the groups. And we make them to suit the question we are asking.

A gardener may sort plants by height. That helps a gardening question. A doctor may sort plants by which ones are used as medicine. That helps a different question. Both sortings are useful. Neither one is the "true" grouping of plants.

Scientists look for a grouping that is useful again and again. The best kind is this: when you know that something belongs to a group, you can say several other things about it. You will meet a grouping like that later in this chapter. Watch for it.
Your school library keeps books in a certain order. What is easy to find because of that order? What is hard to find?
A useful rule must be clear enough for someone else to use. “Plants I like” depends on the person doing the sorting. “Plants with woody stems” asks everyone to inspect the same feature.

Also separate an observation from a guess. “No flowers seen today” is an observation. “This plant never flowers” is a much bigger claim. You would need evidence from other times of year before putting the plant in that group.
A good grouping invites you to check its rule against a new example.
2.2.1 Grouping Plants
Look at Table 2.1 again. The features you wrote there — stem, leaves, flowers — are the same features we can use to sort plants.
Begin with the stem. It is the easiest one to test with your hands.

The setup
**What to do:**
1. Go out to the same place as before. Choose six plants of clearly different sizes.
2. Stand next to each one. Is it shorter than you, about your height, or taller?
3. Look at the stem near the ground. Is it green or brown?
4. Bend the stem very gently with one finger. Does it bend, or is it stiff? **Stop as soon as you feel it resist. A broken stem can kill the plant.**
5. See where the branches start. Near the ground, or higher up?
6. Use the headings in Table 2.3 to make your own notebook table. Leave the last column empty for now.
Before you fill the last column, guess which plants will end up in the same group.
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.

Table 2.3: Grouping plants by height and stem
Plant | Height compared with you | Stem colour | Stem texture | Branching | Group
Mango | Taller | Brown | Hard | High | Tree
Rose | About the same | Brown | Hard | Low | Shrub
Tomato | Shorter | Green | Soft | Low | Herb
Herbs, Shrubs and Trees
Read down your table. Three groups appear on their own.
Some plants are small. They have soft green stems that bend easily. These are called **herbs**. A tomato plant is a herb. So are mint and coriander, and most small plants in an open field.

Some plants are taller. They have several hard brown stems. The branches start close to the ground. These stems are not as thick or as tall as a tree's. Such plants are called **shrubs**. A rose plant is a shrub.
Some plants grow very tall. They have one thick, hard, brown stem. The branches start well above the ground. These are **trees**. A mango is a tree.

Now think about what the stem has to do. A tomato plant holds up a few leaves and some fruit. A mango tree holds up a heavy top of branches, ten metres above the ground, for many years, through wind and rain. A soft green stem could never do that job.
Mango · tree                 Rose · shrub                 Tomato · herb
**Can you explain why?** A banana plant is taller than you and its stem is thick. But the stem is soft and green. Which group does it belong to?
Height alone is not enough. Compare a young mango plant with a mature tomato plant: their present heights may be similar, but their stems and later growth differ.
Plants That Cannot Stand Up
Not every plant can hold itself up.

Some plants have stems that are too weak to stand. So they climb up something else — a wall, a fence, a stick, or another plant. These are called **climbers**. A money plant is a climber. So is a grape vine.
Other plants also have weak stems. But instead of climbing, they spread flat along the ground. These are called **creepers**. Pumpkin and watermelon plants are creepers.

Both kinds have the same problem. A weak stem cannot lift leaves up to the sunlight. A climber solves this by using another plant's height. A creeper solves it in a different way. It gives up on height and spreads sideways instead.
Climber · grape vine                       Creeper · pumpkin
A climber and a creeper both have stems that need support or spread along the ground. What observations would you need before deciding which receives more light?
So far you have grouped plants using only the stem. Leaves give us another way to sort the same plants. That way turns out to be more useful.
Lines on a Leaf
Hold a leaf up against the light. You will see thin lines running through it. These lines are **veins**. The pattern the veins make is called **venation**.
Veins are not just for decoration. They are pipes. They carry water into the leaf, and carry food away from it. They also make the leaf stiff, so it holds its shape instead of hanging loose.

The setup
**You will need:** fallen leaves of at least four different plants, thin paper, a pencil with soft lead.
**What to do:**
1. Put a leaf on the desk with its back side facing up. The veins stand out more on that side.
2. Place a sheet of thin paper over the leaf.
3. Hold the paper still. Rub the side of the pencil lead flat across it, using light strokes.
4. The pattern of veins will appear on the paper.
5. Do this for every leaf. Write the plant's name next to each print.
Put all your prints side by side. Sort your prints into two piles, using the pattern only. What rule did you use?

Choose leaves whose veins are easy to feel. If a print looks faint, first check that the raised veins face the paper and that the paper is held still. A poor print need not mean that the leaf has no veins.
Try the same method on another leaf before changing how you make the print. Compare the patterns, not just their darkness.
Two Patterns
Compare the leaves you printed. Two common patterns help describe many flowering plants, but a small sample cannot establish a rule for every leaf.

In some leaves, one thick vein runs down the middle. Thinner veins branch off it on both sides. Those branch again, and again, until the whole leaf is covered with a net. This pattern is called **reticulate venation**. You can see it clearly in a hibiscus leaf. Mango, neem and peepal leaves have it too.

In other leaves, many veins run alongside one another. This pattern is called **parallel venation**. In a grass blade they run along the length of the leaf. A banana leaf has a strong middle vein, with many parallel side veins running out towards its edges. Parallel venation does not mean that a leaf has no middle vein.
Hibiscus · reticulate             Banana · parallel             Grass · parallel
These two patterns help you compare many of the leaves around you. Look closely: real leaves sometimes show exceptions.
**What do you predict?** Maize and wheat both have long thin leaves, like grass. What venation would you expect in them?
Keep that answer in your mind. We are now going to look at a part of the plant you cannot see at all.
Under the Ground
Roots do two jobs. They hold the plant firmly in place against wind and rain. They take up water and dissolved minerals from the soil.
Roots are buried, so most people never see them. But roots differ from plant to plant, just as leaves do. And you can watch them grow yourself.

The setup
**You will need:** a handful of chana (chickpea) seeds, a handful of wheat or maize seeds, two shallow trays or plates, cotton cloth or cotton wool, water.
**What to do:**
1. Soak both kinds of seed in water overnight.
2. Spread a wet cloth in each tray. Put the chana seeds in one tray. Put the wheat seeds in the other.
3. Keep the cloth wet for the next five or six days. Wet, not flooded. Check it every morning.
4. From day three, take out one seed from each tray every day. Look at what has grown from it.
5. On day six, wash the roots gently. Lay them on paper, side by side.

Draw what grew from each kind of seed in your notebook. Use the same scale for both drawings. Could drawings alone tell you which plant is harder to pull out? What would you need to keep alike in a comparison of root anchorage?
Two Kinds of Root
Your two trays will have grown two very different things.

From the chana seed, one thick root will have gone straight down. Much thinner roots will have branched off it. That main root is called a **taproot**. Mustard, hibiscus, mango and radish all have taproots. In fact, a radish *is* a taproot. It is swollen with stored food. That is why we eat it.

As the wheat seedling develops, several thin roots appear. Later, more roots grow from the base of the stem, forming a spreading bunch without one dominant main root. These are called **fibrous roots**. Grass, maize and lemongrass have them.
Chana · taproot                              Wheat · fibrous roots
The two shapes do two different jobs.
A taproot can grow deep and reach water below the surface. A deep root system can help a plant through a dry spell, although root depth also depends on the species and the soil.
Many fibrous root systems spread through the upper soil. A dense network helps hold loose soil together and take up water near the surface. Some fibrous roots also reach deep into the ground.
A Pattern Appears
You now know two ways to sort plants. One uses leaves. One uses roots.
Leaves are above the ground. Roots are below it. There seems to be no reason why one should tell you anything about the other.
Let us test that.

The setup
**What to do:**
1. Choose five plants you can see fully, roots and all. Young seedlings from a nursery tray work best.
2. For each plant, look at the leaf first. Write down its venation.
3. **Now, before you look at the roots, guess** whether it will have a taproot or fibrous roots. Write your guess down.
4. Then look at the roots. Write down what you actually find.
5. Plant the seedlings back carefully afterwards.
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.

Table 2.4: Leaf venation and root type
Plant | Venation | Root — my guess | Root — what I found
Lemongrass | Parallel |  | Fibrous
How many of your five guesses were right? If you had to guess for a sixth plant now, would you feel more sure?
The Two Go Together
Compare answers across the whole class. The pattern is easy to see.

Plants with reticulate venation almost always have a taproot.
Plants with parallel venation almost always have fibrous roots.
*Sadabahar* has net-like veins and a taproot. Chana has net-like veins and a taproot. Lemongrass has parallel veins and fibrous roots. Wheat has parallel veins and fibrous roots.
Notice the word *almost*. A rule that is true nearly every time is still very useful. But we should say "almost always", not "always". That is more honest.
Now a question should be troubling you. Why should the veins in a leaf have anything to do with the shape of a root? They are at opposite ends of the plant.
The answer is not in the leaf. It is not in the root. It is in the seed.

The setup
**What to do:**
1. Soak a few chana seeds and a few maize seeds in water for two days, until they are soft and swollen.
2. Peel the thin outer coat off a soaked chana. Now try to split the seed with your thumbnail.
3. Try to split a soaked maize seed in the same way.
Which seed comes apart neatly into two halves? Which one does not?
What Is Inside a Seed

A soaked chana splits neatly into two equal halves. Each half is called a **cotyledon**. Look carefully between the two halves. You will see a tiny root and a tiny shoot already formed. That is the start of the new plant, with food packed around it.
A maize grain does not separate into two large cotyledons like chana. Its single cotyledon is visible in the cut-open diagram. Failure to split a seed is not itself proof of its cotyledon count.
This gives us a third way to sort plants. And this one explains the other two.

Plants whose seeds have two cotyledons are called **dicotyledons**. We say **dicots** for short.
Plants whose seeds have one cotyledon are called **monocotyledons**, or **monocots**.
Chana · two cotyledons                         Maize · one cotyledon
Now put all three findings together.

Comparing flowering plants — typical features
 | Dicots | Monocots
Cotyledons in the seed | Two | One
Leaf venation | Reticulate | Parallel
Roots | Taproot | Fibrous
Examples | Chana, mustard, hibiscus, mango | Wheat, maize, grass, banana
This is the grouping worth having. Split one seed, and you can say two more things about a plant you have never seen before.
That is what makes a grouping really useful. It lets you say something new. It does not just tidy up what you already knew.
2.2.2 Grouping Animals
Animals vary as much as plants do. So the same question comes up. Which feature should we use to group them?
Colour is easy to see, but it tells us very little. Size is not much better. A big animal and a small one may live in exactly the same way.
A better starting point is something you have already written down in Table 2.2 — how the animal moves.

List every animal from Table 2.2. Add any others you know well. For each one, write how it moves and which body part it uses. Use Table 2.5 as a guide for your notebook table. Now sort your animals into groups, using the "body part" column only.
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.

Table 2.5: How animals move
Animal | How it moves | Body part used
Ant | Walks | Legs
Goat | Walks and jumps | Legs
Pigeon | Walks and flies | Legs and wings
Housefly | Walks and flies | Legs and wings
Fish | Swims | Fins
Earthworm |  |
Some animals use more than one body part. They will fall into more than one group. Is that a problem with the animals, or with the grouping?
What Movement Tells Us
Animals move in many ways. They walk, run, hop, crawl, fly, swim and glide. Some do more than one, like a pigeon.

Sorting them this way shows us something interesting. Animals that are not alike at all may still move in the same way, using similar body parts. A housefly and a pigeon are very different creatures. But both have wings, and both fly. A fish and a dolphin look alike in water, even though a dolphin is not a fish.
That is a clue about something you will meet soon in this chapter. The way an animal is built has a lot to do with *where* it lives.

Movement is not the only way to group animals. We can also group them by what they eat, by where they live, or by what covers the body — scales, feathers, fur, or nothing at all. As with plants, the best grouping depends on the question we are asking.
Know a scientist

**Janaki Ammal (1897–1984)** was one of the first Indian women to work as a professional botanist. She studied sugarcane and worked on making plant varieties better. In 1952 she became Officer on Special Duty at the Botanical Survey of India and helped reorganise its work. In her eighties she joined the fight to save the forest at Silent Valley in Kerala. Her whole life was spent doing the two things this chapter is about — looking closely at plants, and finding order in what she saw.
2.3 Living Things and Their Surroundings

Something in your tables may have struck you already. The living things you wrote down are the ones that live *here*. A class in Ladakh would fill in a completely different table. So would a class in the Sundarbans, or on the coast of Kerala.
Why? Why do different places have different living things?

Copy Table 2.6 onto the blackboard. As a class, fill it with plants and animals you have seen, read about, or heard about at home. Now look at each column. Ask: what is that place like? Hot or cold? Wet or dry? Windy? Is water easy to find there?
Copy the headings into your notebook and add your own observations. The rows below are examples, not a complete record.

Table 2.6: Living things in different surroundings
Desert | Mountains | Ocean | Forest | Other region
Camel | Deodar tree | Fish | Tiger |
Take any one animal from the desert column. What would happen to it in the conditions of the mountain column?
Some living things occur in several surroundings; others have a much narrower range. Compare the conditions in each column. The features of a living thing help explain where it can survive.
Built for the Place
Look at a plant from a hot desert.

Water is hard to find there. The sun is very strong all day. The nights turn cold. A cactus meets all this with a thick, fleshy stem. The stem stores water through the long dry spells. Its outer surface is tough, so very little water escapes. Its leaves are only spines. A spine loses far less water than a wide flat leaf would.
Now look at a deodar tree, high in the Himalayas.

Here the problem is not heat. It is snow. Snow piling up on branches gets heavy enough to break them. A deodar is shaped like a cone. Its branches slope downward and bend easily. So the snow slides off instead of piling up.
Cactus · hot desert                         Deodar · cold mountain
Neither plant chose its shape. But each one has features that suit the place it grows in. Plants without those features do not last long there.
**Can you explain why?** A cactus planted on a Himalayan slope would probably die. Give two reasons from what you have just read.
The Same Animal, Two Deserts
The clearest example of this is an animal you already know well.

Camels live in the hot sandy desert of Rajasthan. Camels also live in the cold, high, rocky desert of Ladakh. Both places are deserts. Both are dry, with little food and little shelter. But they are dry in very different ways. And the two camels are not the same.
The Rajasthan camel is tall, with long legs. Its two-toed feet have broad, spreading pads. They spread its weight, so it does not sink into loose sand. It has one hump. Its coat is thin.

The Ladakh camel is shorter and heavier. Its sturdy legs also end in broad, padded, two-toed feet. It has two humps. It grows a thick shaggy coat, especially at the head and neck, for winters that fall far below freezing.
Dromedary · one hump                         Bactrian · two humps

You may have heard that a camel stores water in its hump. That is not true. The hump stores fat. The camel lives off that fat when there is no food. By the end of winter, the humps of a Ladakh camel become smaller and lean over to one side.

Camels save water in other ways. They pass very little urine. Their dung is dry enough to burn. They can allow their body temperature to rise during the day, reducing the water needed for cooling. They do sweat when necessary. So a camel can go many days without drinking.
Adaptations
The cactus stem, the deodar's sloping branches, the camel's padded feet and hump — all of these are examples of one idea.

Inherited features that help organisms survive and reproduce in their usual environment are called **adaptations**. They develop in populations over generations; an individual does not acquire a needed feature simply by trying.

Adaptations are not always about extreme places, and they are not always easy to spot. A fish has a smooth body that slips through water easily, and fins to steer and push with. A duck has skin joining its toes. That turns each foot into a paddle. A pigeon's foot has no such skin, because a pigeon is not a swimmer.

Rhododendrons include low shrubs and tall trees in different mountain regions. Their features reflect both inherited differences and growing conditions. Even plants of the same species may grow differently in a windy, exposed place and in a sheltered one. A change in one plant's growth is not the same as an inherited adaptation developing over generations.
**What do you predict?** One plant grows on a windy seashore. The same kind of plant grows in a sheltered valley. Which one would you expect to be taller?
Duck · webbed foot                            Pigeon · no webbing
Habitat
The place where a living thing lives is called its **habitat**.

A habitat gives a plant or animal what it needs — food, water, air, shelter, and a safe place for its young. The habitat of a camel is the desert. The habitat of a sea turtle is the ocean. The habitat of a rhododendron is the mountains.
Many different living things share one habitat. That is why habitats are where we find biodiversity.
Habitats can be sorted into two broad kinds.
Living things on land live in **terrestrial** habitats. Forests, deserts, grasslands and mountains are terrestrial habitats. So is the ground under your feet.
Living things in water live in **aquatic** habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

Some animals use both land and water. Frogs belong to a group called **amphibians**; many amphibians spend part of their lives in each. But using both habitats does not make every animal an amphibian. A crocodile does so too, and it is a reptile.
Know a scientist

**Salim Ali (1896–1987)** spent many years travelling across India, watching birds. He recorded where they lived, when they arrived, and where they went next. Watching carefully like this, year after year, is how scattered sightings turn into real knowledge. His fieldwork and advocacy helped strengthen bird conservation in India. His books also made it possible for ordinary people to name the birds around them. He is remembered as the Birdman of India.
When a Habitat Is Lost
Ask your parents, your grandparents, or an older neighbour one simple question. Which birds, insects or plants did they see often as children, but rarely see now?
Many of them will be able to name several.

When a habitat is damaged or destroyed, the living things there lose everything at once — their food, their shelter, and the place where they raise their young. They usually cannot move somewhere else, because there is often nowhere else that suits them. They simply become fewer. Then they are gone. This is how biodiversity is lost.

Habitat loss has threatened animals such as the Bengal tiger and the Great Indian bustard. Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats. The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952; a reintroduction programme began in 2022. Protecting suitable habitat is essential to conservation.

Governments are not the only ones who protect habitats. **Sacred groves** are patches of forest that communities across India have left untouched for many generations. Nobody cuts trees there. Nobody hunts. Some groves are tiny and some are large. Many hold rare plants that have disappeared from the land all around them. Community traditions and agreements protect many groves; some also have legal protection. Find out if there is one near you. A sacred grove — a surviving patch of forest
Keywords

Adaptation · Amphibian · Aquatic · Biodiversity · Climber · Cotyledon · Creeper · Dicot · Fibrous root · Grouping · Habitat · Herb · Monocot · Parallel venation · Reticulate venation · Sacred grove · Shrub · Taproot · Terrestrial · Tree · Venation
Summary
• The variety of living things found in a region is called its biodiversity. Even an ordinary place has much more of it than a quick look suggests.
• Living things in a place depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs.
• Grouping means arranging things by the features they share. There is no one correct grouping. The useful one depends on the question being asked.
• Plants can be grouped by stem and height into herbs, shrubs and trees. Plants with weak stems are climbers or creepers.
• The pattern of veins in a leaf is called venation. Two common patterns are reticulate and parallel.
• Roots are of two kinds. A taproot has one main root. Fibrous roots form a spreading bunch.
• Among flowering plants, dicots have two cotyledons and monocots have one.

• These three features go together. Dicots generally have reticulate venation and a taproot. Monocots generally have parallel venation and fibrous roots. This is what makes the grouping useful — one observation lets you predict others.
• Animals can be grouped by how they move and which body parts they use. They can also be grouped in many other ways.
• Features that make a living thing fit to survive in a particular place are called adaptations.
• The place where a living thing lives is its habitat. Habitats are terrestrial or aquatic. Many amphibians use both land and water, but not all animals that do so are amphibians.
• Damage to habitats causes loss of biodiversity. This is why habitats are protected — by governments, and by communities.
Let Us Enhance Our Learning
**1.** Here are two seeds — a wheat grain and a kidney bean. Without planting either one, say what kind of root and what kind of leaf venation each plant will have. Explain how you decided.

Learning Further

• Walk around your school with your teacher or the gardener. Label the plants with their local names. Make a list in your notebook. Next to each name, write its group — herb, shrub, tree, climber or creeper.

• Over one term, build a **class biodiversity register**. Every student adds what they see on field visits and on the way to school. Write the date and the place each time. A register kept for several years becomes very valuable, because it shows what is disappearing.
• Talk to the oldest person you know well. Ask which plants, birds and insects were common when they were your age. Write down what they say. Then find out what has changed in that area since then.
• Find out if there is a sacred grove, a protected forest or a bird sanctuary near your district. Who protects it? What is it being protected from?

• Read about one Indian scientist working on biodiversity today. Write a short report. You could start with Divya Mudappa, Vidya Athreya, Uma Ramakrishnan, Nandini Velho, Ghazala Shahabuddin, Usha Lachungpa or Divya Karnad.

• Grow chana and wheat again. For each kind of seed, keep one tray in bright light and another in a dark cupboard. Water all trays equally. Predict what will happen before you start. Then record what actually happens.
